title: Relative use of workers and equipment

blocks.heading: Relative use of workers and equipment
blocks.text: Labour-intensive production relies relatively heavily on labour, while capital-intensive production relies relatively heavily on capital equipment. Intensity compares the input mix, not whether workers or machines are present at all and not simply the sophistication of technology. A process can use many workers and still be capital-intensive relative to an alternative with little equipment. Compare methods for the same task. Availability, skills, cost, output requirements and maintenance influence which mix fits; a labour-intensive method is not automatically the socially or economically best option.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Labour-intensive production
blocks.text: Labour-intensive production is production that relies relatively heavily on labour compared with capital equipment. It may suit tasks using available skills and limited equipment, but capacity, labour time and output quality still matter. A small batch of individually fitted products may use hand skills for adjustments. This is a relative description of inputs, not a claim that no tools are used. To justify the choice, connect the available workers and product requirements to the method.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Capital-intensive production
blocks.text: Capital-intensive production is production that relies relatively heavily on capital equipment compared with labour. It may provide high or consistent output where equipment, demand, power and maintenance are sufficient, but needs investment and suitable support. An automated packaging line still requires people to operate, supervise and maintain it. The presence of workers does not make it labour-intensive. Equally, a single simple tool does not establish capital intensity. Compare relative reliance on the productive assets.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Match intensity to resources
blocks.text: A fictional group receives a small order for individually fitted items. It has skilled workers and hand tools, limited investment finance and no power for an automated line. A relatively labour-intensive method may fit those constraints. This does not establish that complex equipment is necessarily capital-intensive or inappropriate everywhere. Input intensity asks how heavily production relies on workers relative to equipment; complexity asks how sophisticated the tools or systems are. They are separate descriptions.
